newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Informal balloting on candidates for top U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: Informal balloting on candidates for top U.N. post.

text.p: The Security Council holds informal balloting late on Tuesday to test the popularity of four declared candidates vying to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. secretary-general.

At least two rounds of secret voting were expected. The first would register simply a yes, no or abstention. The second would involve the use of specially marked ballots for the five permanent members of the council -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- so that a negative vote by any of them would indicate a veto.

If one or more candidates obtained at least nine votes and avoided a veto, the council could proceed at a later date to a formal vote to nominate one of them for formal approval by the 185-nation General Assembly.

The four declared candidates are Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast; and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former U.N. special envoy for Burundi who now heads the Washington-based Global Coalition for Africa.

Boutros-Ghali, who was vetoed by the United States in a Nov. 19 vote in which all the other 14 council members supported him, suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4. He could reactivate it at any time but if he does he is all but certain to encounter another veto by the United States, which insists the United Nations needs new leadership to implement reforms.

All the candidates so far are from Africa. The council is giving that continent priority on the grounds that if the U.S. veto denies the Egyptian incumbent the second term enjoyed by his predecessors his successor should be another African.

Several other potential African candidates have been the subject of speculation. They include Salim A. Salim, the secretary-general of the Organisation of Africa Unity, and Senegalese Foreign Minister Moustapha Niasse.
South African President Nelson Mandela said last weekend that French President Jacques Chirac had told him France would veto Salim because of an inadequate command of French.
Niasse could face Chinese opposition because of Senegal's ties with Taiwan.
